title: The Cones Of Dunshire

jokes.text: The last time he was in between jobs, he got deep into claymation, so this should be different, hopefully.
jokes.setup: Ben announces he has a week off between jobs and has been 'cooking up something pretty big,' implying exciting news.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's talking-head reveals the last time he had free time he spiraled into claymation, undercutting any optimism with 'hopefully.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Parks cold-open beat. The specificity of 'claymation' is delightfully odd, and Leslie's quiet dread expressed as cautious optimism is perfectly in character. 'Hopefully' does tremendous work as an understatement.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So what are you working on during your week off?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm thinking about starting a consulting firm. Help small businesses with their finances and operations.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's great. Last time you had a week off, you made that claymation movie about a snail.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That was a really good snail, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was. But I'm hoping this is different.

jokes.text: Presenting 'The Cones of Dunshire,' a brand-new gaming experience. 8 to 12 players.
jokes.setup: Ben has been building something in his week off. The reveal is expected to be impressive.
jokes.punchline: It's a wildly overcomplicated board game requiring 8-12 players, immediately signaling absurd overambition.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's central comedic premise and it works brilliantly because it is so deeply Ben Wyatt. Only this character — a former Ice Town mayor, accounting nerd, and fantasy-game obsessive — would spend a week inventing a game with 8-12 players as its baseline requirement. The name 'Cones of Dunshire' is inspired nonsense. Scores high on character integration above all else.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, I've been working on something during my unemployment. It's a board game.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's called 'Cones of Dunshire.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It has a variable player count of two to four players, but theoretically up to six with the expansion pack I'm working on.

jokes.text: Two wizards, a Maverick, the arbiter, two warriors, a corporal, and a ledgerman. Now, the ledgerman just keeps score, and he wears this hat. Oh, boy.
jokes.setup: Ben is explaining the elaborate character roles in his new game with total earnestness.
jokes.punchline: The roles escalate in absurdity — culminating in 'ledgerman,' whose only job is keeping score and wearing a specific hat. Leslie's deadpan 'Oh, boy' is the audience surrogate reaction.
jokes.explanation: The ledgerman detail is the perfect comedic peak of the role-list: after wizards and warriors (genre-standard), 'ledgerman just keeps score and wears this hat' deflates all the fantasy gravitas into mundane bureaucracy. Ben's nerd tendencies literalized: even in fantasy, someone has to do the accounting. Leslie's 'Oh, boy' is pitch-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The ledgerman has a special hat just for keeping score.

jokes.text: The object is to accumulate cones. Four cones wins, but in order to get a cone, you have to build a civilization.
jokes.setup: Ben explains the win condition of his game as if it's perfectly reasonable.
jokes.punchline: To win four cones, you must BUILD A CIVILIZATION — the gap between the trivial goal (cones) and the epic requirement (civilization) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Superb economy: the joke is in the disproportion. 'Accumulate cones' sounds trivial; 'build a civilization' is operatic. The juxtaposition is the comedy, delivered with total Ben-sincerity. Highly quotable precisely because it sounds so deranged out of context.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The ledgerman's hat is actually a crucial part of the ensemble. You see, the brim helps shield the eyes from the sun while you're reviewing the ledger, and the crown provides optimal ventilation for extended periods of accounting work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, there is no ledgerman's hat.

jokes.text: Actually, let me tell you more about the trivia cards, 'cause you're gonna need to know about roadblocks first. Nah, never mind.
jokes.setup: Ben tries to explain the challenge play mechanic.
jokes.punchline: He derails himself with prerequisites to the prerequisites, then abandons the thread entirely — demonstrating the game is too complicated to even explain.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — the recursion of needing to explain things before explaining things is both funny and very true to overly-complicated hobbyist games. Ben's 'nah, never mind' is endearing self-awareness that doesn't quite break the earnest bubble.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, so the way the game works is you roll the dice to determine what you do, and then you roll other dice to determine the outcome of that action.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But then you need to roll dice to determine which dice you actually rolled, so you roll a die to see what the first die was supposed to be.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And if that die contradicts the other die, you roll another die to determine which die is correct.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So basically you're just rolling dice to figure out what dice you rolled. It's elegant, really.

jokes.text: Then you roll three dice to see how many dice you roll with.
jokes.setup: Ben explains the turn mechanics.
jokes.punchline: You roll dice to determine how many dice to roll — recursive absurdity that perfectly captures overcomplicated game design.
jokes.explanation: This is the single sharpest line in the Cones of Dunshire sequence. The recursive dice mechanic is both a perfect parody of overcomplicated Eurogames AND a distillation of the joke into maximum economy. Seven words. Anyone who has played Arkham Horror or Twilight Imperium immediately recognizes the truth in it. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: They're traffic cones.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What do you think they represent?

jokes.text: Oh, 16. Perfect, lots of choices.
jokes.setup: He rolls the three dice to demonstrate how many dice you then roll.
jokes.punchline: Getting 16 — an absurdly high number of dice choices — and greeting it with calm satisfaction, as if this is manageable.
jokes.explanation: The enthusiasm for '16' as 'lots of choices' — presented as a feature not a bug — is a perfect capper to the dice joke. Ben's total absence of self-awareness is what sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So you roll the dice, move your piece around the board, collect resource cards based on where you land, then you trade those cards with other players to build structures, but only if you have the required combination and you're on a designated trading post, which rotates every three turns...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. This needs something. It's not complicated enough.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, now every resource card has a secondary action value on the back, so when you're NOT using it for trading, you can flip it over and use it as a modifier for your movement roll, but only on even-numbered turns, and only if you're wearing the ceremonial sash I'm going to add.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Perfect. That's perfect.

jokes.text: Are the cones a metaphor? Well, yes and no.
jokes.setup: Someone (presumably Leslie) asks if the cones have symbolic meaning.
jokes.punchline: Ben's answer — 'yes and no' — treats a ridiculous question with complete philosophical seriousness, implying he has actually thought this through.
jokes.explanation: Four words that suggest enormous depth of delusion. 'Yes and no' implies Ben has a whole metaphysical framework for his cone symbolism but won't get into it right now. Perfect economy and deeply character-specific — only someone who built an 8-12 player civilization game for fun would answer this way.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I spent a week on this game and I'm ready to throw it in the trash the second we have to go back to work.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, the Maverick should be able to trade lumber for agriculture credits. How have I not thought of this before?
jokes.setup: Ben is mid-explanation of his game.
jokes.punchline: He interrupts himself with a sudden game design breakthrough, horrified he missed it — demonstrating he is still actively in the creative process and the game is unfinished.
jokes.explanation: The game isn't just complicated — it's UNFINISHED and still evolving in real time. Ben's existential distress at the discovery adds a layer to his character. Also a Catan reference that will land well with the target audience.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Leslie can't make decisions anymore because she has what we in politics call 'Stanky boot.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's not a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: It's a very real condition. Look it up.

jokes.text: This is nothing, right? When do you go back to work again? Tomorrow. It's fine. I'll just throw this in the garbage.
jokes.setup: After Ben's elaborate and unhinged game presentation, Leslie is clearly processing how to respond supportively.
jokes.punchline: Ben preemptively deflates the whole thing with 'I'll just throw this in the garbage' — a sad, self-aware beat that shows he knows it's too much, delivered with zero drama.
jokes.explanation: The emotional capper to the Cones of Dunshire cold open. 'I'll just throw this in the garbage' is delivered with maximum deadpan sadness, and works as both a joke and a small character moment about Ben's pattern of manic hobby episodes. The warmth of the scene underlines rather than undercuts the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: You think I'd misuse funds?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, not at all.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But now that you mention it... yes. Yes, I do.

jokes.text: As soon as Knope is gone, these are going up all over Chambers. Jamm for three!
jokes.setup: City council is in session; Jamm is ostensibly a professional.
jokes.punchline: Jamm is already planning self-promotional signage for the moment Leslie leaves, celebrating with a sports reference during official proceedings.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy for Jamm — his pettiness and vanity are well-established, and 'Jamm for three' captures both his sports-referencing swagger and his gleeful anticipation. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Three-bedroom house. Plenty of land. Wood inside.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I think your listing might be a little too detailed. Maybe try shortening it?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: House.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: There we go. That's perfect.

jokes.text: What, are you trying to build a house with those bricks?
jokes.setup: Jamm is trash-talking during what appears to be a game of some kind at council.
jokes.punchline: The sports/game trash talk is aggressively juvenile for a city council chamber, delivered with apparent self-satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: Weak joke on its own — generic sports trash talk. Its value is entirely contextual (city council setting). The line itself isn't clever, but Jamm's character carries it to functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've listed my house for sale. Here are some of the listing details I've included.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Large lot. Room for a man to work. Dead animals for practical purposes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Some might say the dead animals are a drawback. I disagree.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: As a compromise, I've agreed to have the shells cleaned. But the animals stay.

jokes.text: The money for the Pawnee Commons, aka the greatest future park in the world, aka my personal dream project... Aka...
jokes.setup: Leslie raises the Pawnee Commons fund in council. She starts to describe it.
jokes.punchline: She cannot stop 'aka'-ing, building superlatives upon superlatives, and then trails off on a third 'aka' with nothing left to add — showing her passionate inability to speak plainly about her projects.
jokes.explanation: The trailing 'Aka...' that goes nowhere is a nice structural gag. It's pure Leslie Knope — her inability to speak simply about things she loves. Character-specific and economical in the moment, though not a standout line.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've removed the bodies from the property, as requested. They're in a storage unit now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, what? No! You can't just move them!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm willing to compromise. I'll keep the skeletons for composting purposes. Excellent for the garden.

jokes.text: Because the voters, to use a technical political term, gave you the stanky boot.
jokes.setup: Jamm is explaining that Leslie no longer has authority over the fund because she lost her council seat.
jokes.punchline: 'The stanky boot' presented as a 'technical political term' — the absurd slang dressed up in bureaucratic language is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Strong Jamm line. The phrase 'stanky boot' is both hilariously crude and weirdly apt as a metaphor for electoral defeat. Framing it as a 'technical political term' is the structural move that elevates it from mere slang. Highly quotable and very Jamm-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I've started my own real estate business. It's called Donna Meagle's Marvelous Meagle Mansions.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: My slogan is: 'Donna Meagle's Marvelous Meagle Mansions: Making Magical Memories in Meagle Manner.'

jokes.text: But we'll keep your money safe, baby girl.
jokes.setup: Jamm is ostensibly being reassuring to Leslie about the funds.
jokes.punchline: He calls her 'baby girl' in an official council setting — condescending, sexist, and completely tone-deaf, which is exactly Jamm's character.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's patronizing 'baby girl' in a professional setting is cringe comedy done right — it's uncomfortable because it's so recognizable, and it perfectly encapsulates his character's awfulness. Not an original construct but executed with specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I want to be a business mogul. You know, like a skiing mogul, except with business.

jokes.text: What, you think I'm gonna use it to put a new limestone shower in my office? Yeah, now I do.
jokes.setup: Leslie defensively asks if Jamm thinks she'd misuse the funds.
jokes.punchline: Jamm's 'Yeah, now I do' — meaning her raising the specific example of a limestone shower made him think of it — is a sharp comic reversal.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection structure: Leslie names an absurd hypothetical to prove she wouldn't do it, which only plants the seed in Jamm's mind. 'Yeah, now I do' is the perfect tight response. Very clean joke construction.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I've heard great things about you, Ben. People say you're smart, you're dedicated, you're a hard worker. So I'm going to put a lot of pressure on you, and I hope you can handle it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Thanks, I appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm serious. A lot of pressure.

jokes.text: I propose that we table this discussion until, let's say, the second Knope is gone. Later, bunheads.
jokes.setup: Jamm is adjourning the meeting.
jokes.punchline: 'The second Knope is gone' (implying first is right now, verbally dismissing her presence) combined with 'Later, bunheads' — an absurd, contemptuous farewell that's beneath any elected official.
jokes.explanation: 'Bunheads' is a perfect Jamm insult — inexplicably specific, faintly derogatory, and entirely meaningless. The motion to table until 'the second Knope is gone' is a neat bit of Jamm logic. Solid character work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, Ann, I'm so excited for you. I'll call you tomorrow. Bye!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, is Ann okay? I heard she was pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She's fine, Chris. She's really happy about it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great. I was worried she might be in some kind of distress.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, everything's perfect. She's going to be a great mom.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, if there's anything I can do to help, just let me know.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, that's really sweet of you, Chris. I'll definitely—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, did you hear that? Chris said he'd help! Ann? Hello?

jokes.text: Glass! Video Ron demand.
jokes.setup: Tom is doing his Tom Haverford thing — coining phrases and acting like an entrepreneur.
jokes.punchline: 'Video Ron demand' is a portmanteau of 'video on demand' and Ron's name — a pun that implies Ron is some kind of media content available for streaming, delivered with Tom's characteristic self-satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: Tom's wordplay is always character-integrated, and 'Video Ron demand' is a clever pun that works on multiple levels — it's a tech reference, a Ron joke, and pure Tom-speak. The 'Glass!' exclamation before it echoes Google Glass and sets up the gag perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jeremy Jamm has blocked 47 of my initiatives. I've blocked 3 of his. But here's the thing - two of those were just to block him, and one was actually a good initiative that I would've supported if he hadn't supported it first. So really, I've blocked 2 of his initiatives. But I'm still winning because I blocked them more recently, which means I have momentum.

jokes.text: What you carrying, my dude?
jokes.setup: Tom greets Ron in his signature over-familiar street vernacular.
jokes.punchline: The comedy is entirely in Tom addressing the stoic, old-fashioned Ron Swanson with 'my dude' — the register clash between characters.
jokes.explanation: Functional Tom-to-Ron character contrast joke. The humor is in the register mismatch alone. Doesn't rise beyond that premise.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I have a master's degree in public policy from Georgetown. Dr. Phil got his Ph.D. in clinical psychology from a diploma mill in Oklahoma. So I'm basically more qualified than him.

jokes.text: Ron's cabin for-sale ad: 'For sale. Small house. Location: Forest.' 'It's a little wordy, don't you think?'
jokes.setup: Ron has written his own real estate listing.
jokes.punchline: The listing is hilariously sparse and unhelpful ('Location: Forest'), but Tom's response treats it as TOO WORDY — the joke being that Ron's Spartan aesthetic has produced something so minimal that the criticism is purely comedic.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Location: Forest' is inspired — it's technically accurate and completely useless as a real estate descriptor, perfectly embodying Ron's contempt for unnecessary specification. Tom calling it 'wordy' is the perfect inversion: the joke is that even this absurdly minimal listing is too much for Ron's ideal, and Tom's criticism comes from an opposite direction (professional polish) that creates a double absurdity. Very high character integration score — this joke could ONLY be Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm selling my cabin.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, one of my cabins.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have several.

jokes.text: 'Current owner will not clean up shotgun shells or animal carcasses.'
jokes.setup: Tom is reading Ron's cabin listing aloud and critiquing it.
jokes.punchline: Ron has included a disclosure that he won't clean up shotgun shells or animal carcasses — presented as a matter of principle, not embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'shotgun shells OR animal carcasses' — note the 'or,' suggesting both are items requiring individual consideration — is great. Ron treating this as a reasonable disclosure rather than something a sane person would hide is pure character comedy. The line could be embroidered on a pillow and sold at a Ron Swanson gift shop.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My new cabin has several advantages over my current one. Better insulation, more efficient wood stove, and I won't have to replace the bear traps every season.

jokes.text: Fine, I'll clean up the shotgun shells, but the carcasses remain to fertilize my berry patch.
jokes.setup: Tom reacts with horror at the listing's carcass disclosure.
jokes.punchline: Ron's negotiation: he'll concede the shotgun shells but draws a firm line at the carcasses — because they serve a legitimate agricultural purpose (berry patch fertilizer). The logic is internally consistent and completely insane.
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best lines. The revelation that the carcasses have a PURPOSE (berry patch fertilization) recontextualizes everything and makes Ron more, not less, insane. His deadpan negotiating tone — as if this is a normal concession — is perfection. High quotability because it sounds deranged out of context and makes perfect sense in it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So you want to skip the staging process?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't want to skip anything. I want to stand very still and watch the shadows move across the walls.

jokes.text: Spladow! Check it. 'Regal Meagle Realty.' 'Find your castle.'
jokes.setup: Tom suggests Donna could use her real estate license on Ron's cabin.
jokes.punchline: Donna reveals she already has business cards reading 'Regal Meagle Realty' with the tagline 'Find your castle' — the alliteration, the self-mythologizing name, and the regal framing is perfectly Donna.
jokes.explanation: 'Regal Meagle' is great branding comedy — it rhymes, it's vain, and it captures Donna's self-perception perfectly. 'Find your castle' as the tagline for a cabin in the forest is a nice ironic touch. Donna producing pre-made business cards the moment an opportunity arises is also funny business logic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why is everyone being so nice to me? Why are they so interested in my cases? Are they... are they going to kill me?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm too good at this. I solve cases too efficiently. They see me as a threat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I need to start making mistakes. Intentional mistakes. Or I'm a dead man.

jokes.text: ♪ Split that commish
jokes.setup: Donna agrees to split the commission with Tom.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately breaks into an impromptu song celebrating the commission split — 'split that commish' — reducing a professional arrangement to a celebratory jingle.
jokes.explanation: Tom's spontaneous musicality is a well-worn character beat, but 'split that commish' specifically is fresh and funny. The abbreviation 'commish' combined with a rap-style brag about a real estate commission is a characteristically Tom juxtaposition.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: No shoes in the house. That's the rule.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But you're wearing shoes right now.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I live here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So the rule is... no shoes in the house, except for you, who live here?

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Exactly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not a rule. That's just you describing what you're doing right now.

jokes.text: The question I always ask myself is, what kind of mogul should I be? Fashion mogul, energy drink mogul. I even thought about downhill skiing. A mogul mogul.
jokes.setup: Tom is in a talking-head confessional about his ambitions.
jokes.punchline: 'A mogul mogul' — the skiing double-meaning lands perfectly after the setup of listing mogul types. The structure leads you down the list and then snaps back with the wordplay.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best pun, and one of the better wordplay jokes in the series. The structure is meticulous: establish the pattern (mogul = business titan), list several examples, pivot to skiing (which breaks the pattern slightly), then deliver 'a mogul mogul' — which is BOTH the skiing term AND a meta-completion of the mogul-types list. The joke earns the pun through careful setup rather than just announcing it. Tom's deadpan delivery of this as genuine strategic contemplation makes it land even harder.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: This is not sexual. I'm just a fan of golf.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Then why is she in a bikini?

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: I photoshopped that.

jokes.text: That's a hot mogul right now.
jokes.setup: Tom considers real estate as his mogul path.
jokes.punchline: Describing real estate as 'a hot mogul right now' — as if mogul types are trends like seasonal fashion — is pure Tom Haverford market-speak applied to personal identity.
jokes.explanation: A solid capper to the mogul monologue. Tom treating mogul archetypes as trend items is consistent and funny, though it's a lesser beat after the mogul/mogul peak.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, we have sleeping bags, we have snacks, we have a first aid kit, we have a discounted designer skirt with a small stain on the hem and a broken zipper.

jokes.text: Ben Wyatt, reporting for duty. How you doing, Barney? Good to see you again. Dad! He's here! He really came!
jokes.setup: Ben shows up to his new accounting firm on his first day, greeting an old acquaintance.
jokes.punchline: His coworkers react to Ben's arrival with the screaming excitement of teenagers meeting a pop star — 'He really came!' — suggesting Ben has been mythologized at this firm way beyond normal colleague status.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the disproportionate reaction: accountants losing their minds over a colleague's arrival. It establishes that Ben is a legend in accounting circles, which is both absurd and deeply endearing. 'He really came!' has the energy of a Beatles concert.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Look at this table I got! Cost me eight thousand dollars!

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: It's from this exclusive Japanese designer. Hideous, right?

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: But that's what makes it perfect. BANZAI!

jokes.text: I took the job when you passed it up last time. Heard a lot about you. Well, all good things, I hope. A little too good. Let's see if you live up to the hype.
jokes.setup: Frank introduces himself as the person who got Ben's job when Ben turned it down.
jokes.punchline: 'A little too good. Let's see if you live up to the hype.' — Frank positions himself as a rival challenger to Ben's accounting legend status, treating it with the gravity of a sports rivalry.
jokes.explanation: Competent joke that extends the accounting-celebrity gag. Frank's rivalry framing ('live up to the hype') is funny in context but not a standout line. Works best as a continuation of the established bit.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Welcome to my home! I've prepared an authentic Japanese breakfast experience for you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I present to you... *attempts exaggerated accent* ...the traditional Japanese morning feast of eggs, bacon, and toast!

jokes.text: Oh, the father of your child is here. I have to go. I'll talk to you soon. I love you. Was that Ann? I hope you were speaking to her in a calming voice 'cause babies can hear everything.
jokes.setup: Leslie is on the phone with Ann. Chris interrupts.
jokes.punchline: Chris's note that 'babies can hear everything' applied to a phone call Leslie was having — the implication being Leslie's dramatic conversation about Jamm being a 'dinkhead' was somehow audible to an unborn child.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chris Traeger wellness-obsession applied to an absurd context. His concern for fetal auditory exposure to Leslie's passionate phone call is funny and in-character. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hipster Buyer 1
dialogue.line: Oh wow, no electricity? That's so... authentic.

dialogue.speaker: Hipster Buyer 2
dialogue.line: And the outhouse is literally fifty yards away? That's peak meta-cabin.

dialogue.speaker: Hipster Buyer 1
dialogue.line: The inconvenience is actually the whole aesthetic. It's ironic, you know?

dialogue.speaker: Hipster Buyer 2
dialogue.line: Exactly. We'll take it. This is the most meta-cabin ever.

jokes.text: Frank seems cool.
jokes.setup: Frank has just given Ben a barely-veiled competitive challenge.
jokes.punchline: Ben's talking-head assessment 'Frank seems cool' is either totally oblivious to Frank's hostility or a masterpiece of forced positivity — both readings are funny.
jokes.explanation: Three words doing a lot of work. The economy is near-perfect — there's no better way to deliver this joke. The ambiguity between obliviousness and forced positivity is rich. Classic mockumentary talking-head comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This cabin? Totally owned by an obscure folk musician in the '70s. Very indie. Very underground.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The previous owner? He inspired Bon Iver. Well, not directly inspired, but they definitely shared a similar energy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And see this water stain? That's where he spilled artisanal kombucha. Vintage kombucha. Before it was cool.

dialogue.speaker: Potential buyers
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Absolutely. You basically can't get more authentic than this place.

jokes.text: Baby, if you can still hear me, I love you. The phone is hung up. Oh.
jokes.setup: Chris encourages Leslie to speak calmingly to Ann's baby through the phone. Leslie does so.
jokes.punchline: Chris informs her the phone is already hung up. Leslie's 'Oh.' is pure deflation.
jokes.explanation: Tight structure: setup (Chris's concern), buy-in (Leslie talking to disconnected phone), punchline (it's already hung up), reaction ('Oh.'). The efficiency is the strength here — the 'Oh.' is perfectly timed and carries the weight of mild embarrassment without overdoing it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, so I've reviewed the contract terms, and the solution is actually straightforward. We just need to add a severability clause.

dialogue.speaker: Coworker 1
dialogue.line: Wait, what? You solved it?

dialogue.speaker: Coworker 2
dialogue.line: BEN SOLVED IT! BEN SOLVED IT!

dialogue.speaker: Coworker 1
dialogue.line: This is the greatest day of my life!

dialogue.speaker: Coworker 3
dialogue.line: I'm calling my mother! Ben from Parks solved our legal issue!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's really not that—

dialogue.speaker: Coworker 2
dialogue.line: SEVERABILITY CLAUSE! SEVERABILITY CLAUSE!

jokes.text: You got my message about Jamm being a dinkhead? Yes, but as city manager, I can't play sides. And I think all of our heads can be a little dinky at times. Fine, but his is the dinkiest. And I would know because I'm keeping score.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Chris for support against Jamm.
jokes.punchline: Chris offers diplomatic balance; Leslie insists Jamm is uniquely dinky, and reveals she's been keeping score of their council battles.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of 'dinky' to 'dinkiest' and the reveal that Leslie quantifies everything — including interpersonal conflicts — is funny and character-true. Chris's diplomatic 'all of our heads can be a little dinky' is a lovely absurdist note.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: You take the pod, you crack it open with your teeth, and then you swallow the whole thing. Pod and all. That's how they do it in Japan.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm pretty sure you're supposed to squeeze the bean out with your teeth and just eat the bean.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: No, no, no. The pod is the best part. It's got all the fiber.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Right, but it's not edible. The pod is not meant to be eaten.

jokes.text: Ever since I started city council, I have gone head-to-head with Jamm 112 times. He has won 56 times, I have won 56 times. I will not lose our last battle.
jokes.setup: Leslie is making her case for why this matters.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that it is EXACTLY tied — 56-56 out of 112 encounters — is both absurd (that she tracks this) and funny in its cosmic symmetry. It also escalates the stakes comedically.
jokes.explanation: The exactness — 112 encounters, perfectly split — is what makes this funny. Only Leslie Knope would know this number, and only the universe of Parks and Rec would arrange it into a perfect tie right before the final battle. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You know what? Let's call Leslie 'Les-lie... the Lesion.' Get it? Because she's like an infection on this town council.

jokes.text: No. Oh. The way you stood up like that, I thought it was gonna go a different way.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Chris for direct help. He stands up — a physical action that implies he's about to dramatically agree.
jokes.punchline: He says 'No.' The standing was misleading. Leslie's observation that she misread the physical cue is the meta-joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke that only works in a visual medium. Chris stands up — conventional TV grammar for 'I'm about to make a declaration' — then immediately deflates it with 'No.' Leslie articulating the misdirection ('I thought it was gonna go a different way') is both the explanation AND the punchline. It's meta without being aggressively meta. Clean and satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: We could do a Grease duet! You could be Danny Zuko.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm going to play Sandy. My vocal range is much better suited for the female part.

jokes.text: No, I can't help directly, but I am on your side. And I will assist you in any way that I can. Maybe I can mediate, like Dr. Phil, only qualified.
jokes.setup: Chris explains how he can help Leslie while staying neutral.
jokes.punchline: 'Like Dr. Phil, only qualified' — a quick, sharp burn on Dr. Phil that also establishes Chris's own self-regard.
jokes.explanation: Tight four-word punchline. 'Only qualified' does a lot — it's a Dr. Phil dig, a Chris self-compliment, and it lands cleanly. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would pay $200 for this to never happen again.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Actually, I would pay $500.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No wait, $1,000. I would pay $1,000 to make this stop.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Scratch that. I would pay any amount of money. Name it. I will write you a check right now.

jokes.text: Recently, I purchased a new cabin big enough for the whole family. I just can't justify owning four cabins.
jokes.setup: Tom asks if Diane is making Ron sell the cabin.
jokes.punchline: Ron's self-correction — it's not one additional cabin, he now has FOUR, making two a responsible downsizing — delivered with complete calm.
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes in stages: (1) the reveal that Ron owns more than one cabin, (2) the self-correction to 'four,' and (3) his completely reasonable framing that four is too many. 'I just can't justify owning four cabins' is perfect Ron — the issue isn't owning multiple remote survival cabins, it's the extravagance of the fourth. Only Ron Swanson could deliver this with a straight face and make it feel completely plausible.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Glamping is like camping, but with luxury amenities. You know, comfortable beds, heated tents, gourmet meals...

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: So it's a hotel.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, it's different. You're still outside in nature.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's a hotel with extra steps.

jokes.text: Two cabins. / [Ron corrects himself from saying he has 'four cabins']
jokes.setup: Ron says he 'can't justify owning four cabins' — revealing he has multiple properties.
jokes.punchline: An immediate cut to Ron correcting himself to 'two cabins' suggests the true number is somewhere between two and four and that Ron has reasons to be vague about this.
jokes.explanation: This is a lovely mockumentary beat. The cut from 'four cabins' to Ron reconsidering and saying 'two cabins' implies he caught himself revealing too much — either there are indeed four cabins and he doesn't want anyone to know, or the number keeps changing. Either way, it confirms Ron as a man of hidden depths and hidden real estate. Economical, character-perfect, rewatch-worthy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, what you just witnessed is authentic Ron Swanson. He doesn't do small talk, he doesn't do pleasantries, and he certainly doesn't do open houses. But that's what makes this property special. This is a man's home. A real man's home. Built on a foundation of solitude, self-reliance, and a complete disregard for your feelings.

jokes.text: Plus, it doesn't have these razor-sharp perimeter defense planks sticking out of the ground.
jokes.setup: Ron is listing the advantages of his new cabin for the family.
jokes.punchline: He mentions the OLD cabin has 'razor-sharp perimeter defense planks' as a standard feature — a detail so specific and so Ron that it takes a second to process.
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson has RAZOR-SHARP PERIMETER DEFENSE PLANKS around his cabin. The phrase 'perimeter defense' for a residential property is extraordinary. He lists this as a negative for family purposes — not because it exists, but because it's inconvenient with kids. It implies Ron's cabin was designed to repel humans, which tracks perfectly. Highly character-specific and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: You know what? I've decided. In our little superhero dynamic, you're the hero and I'm the villain.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really? Why would you choose to be the villain?

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Because villains are rich. Heroes are always broke, living in studios, driving used cars. Villains have lairs, henchmen, offshore accounts. It's the smart choice.

jokes.text: I usually get a 5% commission, but I'll do it for 3%. Friends and family discount. Make it 5%. I don't want you getting any ideas about us being friends.
jokes.setup: Donna offers Ron a reduced commission as a 'friends and family discount.'
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately insists on paying full price to avoid the implication of friendship — a beautiful inversion of normal negotiation.
jokes.explanation: This joke perfectly captures Ron's commitment to his own emotional philosophy — he won't accept financial generosity if it implies social intimacy. The reversal of normal negotiation (fighting to pay MORE) is structurally elegant. Donna's 'Respect.' suggests even she appreciates the purity of the move. One of the episode's most quotable exchanges.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This isn't even real Japanese food, Jeremy. It's just regular American food with soy sauce dumped all over it.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Well maybe if you had any culinary creativity, you'd appreciate what I'm trying to do here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Culinary creativity? You put sriracha on a hot dog and called it 'Asian fusion.'

jokes.text: For the fireplace, I'm thinking fake antlers. But what kind of scarves do we want to hang off the fake antlers? Oh, duh. Crocheted. Most def. That'll look legit next to those antique 'Visit France' posters.
jokes.setup: Tom and Donna are planning how to stage Ron's cabin for sale.
jokes.punchline: Their staging ideas — fake antlers, crocheted scarves, 'Visit France' posters — are absurdly opposed to the cabin's actual character, demonstrating they have zero understanding of who would buy it.
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Tom and Donna staging Ron's survivalist cabin as a chic urban retreat is solid. 'Most def' and 'legit' applied to decorating choices are pure Tom/Donna voice. 'Visit France posters' is an inspired choice of wrong aesthetic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann Arbor? Really? That's just Ann's name twice. It's like if I moved to a city called Leslie Leslie. Which, okay, would be amazing, but that's not the point. Ann Arbor is basically admitting they have no imagination. They saw Ann and thought, 'You know what this needs? More Ann.'

jokes.text: Ron, you want to stay outside and do nothing while they make your cabin look like garbage? I'd like that very much. We can watch the shadows get longer.
jokes.setup: Tom offers Ron the option to stay outside while they stage the cabin.
jokes.punchline: Ron's enthusiastic 'I'd like that very much' followed by the specific, poetic suggestion to 'watch the shadows get longer' — Ron's idea of recreational bliss is sitting silently and watching time pass.
jokes.explanation: 'We can watch the shadows get longer' is beautiful Ron Swanson poetry. It's not a joke — it's how Ron describes leisure — and that sincerity makes it funnier. The 'I'd like that very much' is a masterclass in Ron's enthusiastic engagement with simple natural pleasures. Deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Michigan? Really? What kind of state looks like a mitten? That's not a state, that's a craft project gone wrong. And don't even get me started on the Upper Peninsula — it's like Michigan couldn't commit to being one thing, so it just split itself in half like some kind of geographical commitment-phobe. It's the only state that requires a map just to understand its own borders!

jokes.text: Three competing family trusts, a contested will — it's a real puzzler! So let's see what you got, genius.
jokes.setup: Ben's first day at the accounting firm; he's been given a challenging case.
jokes.punchline: The coworkers' giddy enthusiasm ('it's a real puzzler!') combined with 'let's see what you got, genius' frames this like a game or talent show, not a professional challenge — the cult-of-Ben energy continues.
jokes.explanation: Extends the accounting-celebrity bit competently. 'It's a real puzzler!' is sweet and slightly unhinged energy from an adult accountant. Functional but not the funniest iteration of this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're like someone who sides with Voldemort, or Thanos, or the Empire in Star Wars.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Well, those are all fictional villains. I'm a real person making real choices.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly! You're choosing to be evil!

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: I'm not evil. And also, Morgan Freeman's voice is overrated.

jokes.text: If I'm murdered tonight, start the investigation with those two guys.
jokes.setup: Ben is left alone to work on the contested will case. His coworkers are watching him with intense anticipation.
jokes.punchline: Ben, clearly unnerved by the staring, addresses the camera with a pre-emptive murder suspect designation — treating the staring as genuinely threatening.
jokes.explanation: Excellent talking-head joke. 'Start the investigation with those two guys' is perfectly constructed — the implication is that their enthusiasm has crossed into the uncanny valley of menace. Economy is nearly perfect (one sentence), and the dark turn from accounting to murder is unexpected and hilarious. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not saying Morgan Freeman doesn't have a nice voice, but let's be honest – it's overrated. Everyone acts like he's God just because he narrates everything. The guy's been in what, a thousand movies? You can't tell me they're all good.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jeremy, Morgan Freeman's voice is literally one of the most beloved things in entertainment.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Exactly. Universally beloved. Which means contrarian me has to hate it.

jokes.text: No shoes, you lose. 'No shoes, you lose'? That means we should have shoes then, right? No shoes...
jokes.setup: Jamm insists on a 'no shoes' rule in his home and states it as 'No shoes, you lose.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately points out that grammatically, 'no shoes, you lose' implies shoes would be the winning condition, defeating the rule's intent. Jamm trails off unable to resolve it.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's logical parsing of Jamm's rhyming house rule is a great joke. The 'snooze you lose' rhyme scheme fails to communicate the intended meaning, and Leslie identifying the flaw punctures Jamm's swagger. Jamm's inability to recover ('No shoes...') is a lovely beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Is that... are those calzones? Oh my God, this is the best day of my life. You guys know me so well. Calzones are literally perfect. They're like pizza, but they're also a sandwich. It's the best of both worlds.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I could eat calzones every single day for the rest of my life and die a happy man.

jokes.text: Yeah, so this is my weekend dojo. Sorry, the place is a bit of a mess. My wife's in Oklahoma for eight months. Maybe forever. We'll see if she forgives me.
jokes.setup: Jamm shows Leslie and Chris into his home.
jokes.punchline: The casual escalation from 'eight months' to 'maybe forever' to 'we'll see if she forgives me' — delivered in the same breezy register — reveals a marital catastrophe Jamm is treating as a minor inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is excellent: 'eight months' (odd but okay), 'maybe forever' (alarming), 'we'll see if she forgives me' (implies something catastrophic, casually mentioned). Classic cringe-comedy revelation building. Jamm's complete equanimity about his abandoned marriage is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Surprise! We threw you a party!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: And we got you a cake!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh wow, thank you guys so much!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, that's not a cake.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's twelve calzones stacked on top of each other.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This is the best day of my life.

jokes.text: Who's that, Michelle Wie? It's not sexual. I'm just a really big fan of her game. Really? Because in that picture, she's wearing a bikini. Yeah, thanks. Photoshopped it myself. Fantastic.
jokes.setup: There is a large framed photo of golfer Michelle Wie on Jamm's wall.
jokes.punchline: Jamm pre-emptively denies it's sexual — which raises the question — then reveals he not only found the picture but PHOTOSHOPPED her into a bikini himself. His 'thanks' in response to Leslie calling it 'fantastic' (clearly sarcastic) adds a final layer.
jokes.explanation: The escalation is perfectly constructed: denial → suspicious framing → revelation that he did the photoshopping himself. The detail that he manually created the image makes it so much worse than if he'd just found it. Leslie's 'Fantastic' as deadpan disgust is an excellent straight-man reaction. One of Jamm's best character moments in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I bought this cabin in 1974 for $400.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wow, that's incredible.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It was a different time. You could get a fully functional cabin, complete with septic system and well water, for the price of a used snowmobile.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well now developers are offering you $3.8 million.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know. It's outrageous. This cabin is worth exactly what I paid for it: $400. Everything else is just noise.

jokes.text: Well, this is about the time I hit the hay, so... Why don't we all hit the hay? We'll stay here, get a good night's sleep, and we can start negotiations tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Jamm tries to end the meeting early by announcing bedtime.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately adopts his framing and escalates it into an overnight stay negotiation tactic — not leaving, just sleeping there.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's pivot to using Jamm's own suggestion as leverage is clever and in character. The audacity of declaring they'll stay is a good escalation of her moxie.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I would use it to isolate and observe spiders in their natural habitat, and document their mating patterns while slowly losing my grip on reality.

jokes.text: We stopped at the outlet mall on the way here. Got ourselves a sleeping bag, a giant tin of caramel corn, and an irregular skirt from DKNY. The hem is crooked, but it was 8 bucks.
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals her team is prepared to stay overnight.
jokes.punchline: The supplies list escalates in oddness — sleeping bag (practical), caramel corn (semi-practical), DKNY irregular skirt (completely unrelated to a negotiation sleepover). The detail about the crooked hem being worth it at $8 is the perfect Leslie tangent.
jokes.explanation: The DKNY skirt is the inspired comedic pivot in this list — it has nothing to do with the overnight negotiation stay and everything to do with Leslie being Leslie. The 8-dollar justification grounds it in real human behavior. Good list construction.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'd use the cabin for baking cookies, reading books by the fireplace, taking long walks through nature, and burying bodies where no one would ever find them.

jokes.text: I got it from an actual Benihana. Cost me 4 grand. Worth every penny. Hai!
jokes.setup: Leslie notices a large Benihana-style teppan table in Jamm's house.
jokes.punchline: Jamm confirms he purchased a hibachi table from a Benihana for $4,000 and performs a performative 'Hai!' — his appropriation of Japanese restaurant culture as personal home décor is absurdly on-brand.
jokes.explanation: The 'actual Benihana' detail — as opposed to a replica or similar product — is important. Jamm went to a Benihana and bought their table. The 'Hai!' is cringe-comedy gold: enthusiastic cultural mimicry with zero self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The cabin will be perfect for weekends, hosting friends, and you know, disposing of bodies if needed. I've already scouted good locations in the woods.

jokes.text: Can I interest anyone in an authentic a-Japanese a-break-a-fast? Scrambled eggs eaten with chopsticks?
jokes.setup: Jamm is performing at the Benihana table for his guests.
jokes.punchline: His idea of 'authentic Japanese breakfast' is scrambled eggs eaten with chopsticks — the fake accent combined with the thoroughly un-Japanese breakfast is layered cringe.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's faux-Japanese phonetics ('a-Japanese a-break-a-fast') layered on scrambled eggs is peak Jamm cultural cluelessness. The specificity of scrambled eggs as the 'authentic' dish makes it funnier — it's the most American possible breakfast presented as Japanese.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm offering $8,000 and this blood pressure cuff I stole from the hospital.

jokes.text: This place is so random. I don't know. It's kind of, like, in the middle of nowhere. I know. That's, like, the hilarious part. It's like a joke how long it takes to get here. It's like a meta-cabin.
jokes.setup: Prospective buyers are touring Ron's remote cabin.
jokes.punchline: The hipsters love the cabin specifically because of its inconvenience and remoteness — calling it 'a meta-cabin.' They've turned Ron's genuine survivalism into an ironic aesthetic.
jokes.explanation: 'Meta-cabin' is a great coinage — the hipsters have reframed Ron's anti-modern fortress as an ironic cultural statement. This is sharp cultural observation comedy about how artisanal/ironic consumption works.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's my inhaler!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, it's not. You left it in the conference room, which is city property. Anything left on city property for more than 24 hours becomes city property. Therefore, it's my inhaler now.

jokes.text: I heard that Dave Eggers wrote a short story about this tape cassette that he found under that tree over there.
jokes.setup: Donna is working the hipster buyers by dropping cultural references.
jokes.punchline: The Dave Eggers story about a tape cassette is entirely fabricated — specific enough to sound credible, absurd enough to be clearly invented — deployed to drive up perceived cultural cachet.
jokes.explanation: The Dave Eggers name-drop with the cassette detail is pitch-perfect hipster bait. The specificity ('under that tree over there') makes it feel like a real anecdote, which is exactly the con Donna is running. Donna's scheming competence is well-showcased.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, you made a deal trading future favors for the lockbox? Chris, you're leaving town in like a week.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I know, but I got the lockbox.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Those favors are worthless now.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, I heard that Neko Case and Ben Gibbard made out here once.
jokes.setup: Donna has established the cabin's fake indie credibility with the Dave Eggers story.
jokes.punchline: She escalates to a romantic indie music anecdote — Neko Case and Ben Gibbard (two actual indie music icons) making out at the cabin — further inflating its cultural mythology.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation from literary (Eggers) to musical (indie icons). The pairing of Neko Case and Ben Gibbard is informed — both are legitimate indie royalty, making this sound credible to the target buyer. Ron's interruption ('What are you doing?') and Donna's honest answer ('Getting these dumdums to pay more money') is a great capper.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Look, I know it wasn't the most ethical thing to do, but I was desperate. Besides, technically, I didn't lie — I just withheld information.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: And in my defense, everyone does this. It's not like I'm the only one who's ever bent the rules a little bit.

jokes.text: I'm trying to get these annoying dumdums to pay more money for your cabin. Carry on.
jokes.setup: Ron catches Donna mid-fabrication and asks what she's doing.
jokes.punchline: Donna's completely honest confession — 'getting these annoying dumdums to pay more money' — combined with Ron's 'Carry on' (approving her scheme) is a lovely beat.
jokes.explanation: 'Annoying dumdums' is a great Donna-ism. Ron's immediate endorsement of mild consumer deception is both in character (he respects straightforward self-interest) and funny as an ethical position. 'Carry on' is perfection.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, you're offering me the city manager job?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yes! You're gonna knock it out of the park, Ben. You're gonna be so good at this. It's gonna be epic and legendary and... flippity-floppity-floop!

jokes.text: You could just open the door and let the actual smell of the pines in. Trees are sticky, and they got bugs in them.
jokes.setup: Donna suggests using a pine-scented candle to evoke the outdoors inside the cabin.
jokes.punchline: Ron suggests simply opening the door to let actual pine smell in. Donna's rebuttal — 'Trees are sticky, and they got bugs in them' — is an absurd dismissal of actual nature in favor of synthetic nature.
jokes.explanation: Donna's preference for fake pine over real pine — in a cabin in the woods — is a beautiful character reversal. 'Trees are sticky, and they got bugs in them' is her sincere objection to nature, which makes it funnier. The comedic tension between Ron (who loves real nature) and Donna (who prefers curated nature) is well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Even my farewell note includes detailed game instructions. 'Step 1: Remove all pieces from the box. Step 2: Organize by color. Step 3: Read the 47-page rulebook. Step 4: Realize you've made a terrible mistake.'

jokes.text: Oh, oh! Ben, Ben. Say it again but this time I'm gonna turn the light on, like you just had an idea. Sure, sure. Yeah, I'm with you. What if we dissolve the trust? Yes!
jokes.setup: After Ben solves the case, a coworker wants to recreate the moment cinematically.
jokes.punchline: The coworker wants to stage Ben's insight as a movie moment with theatrical lighting — and Ben just goes along with it, repeating the line on cue.
jokes.explanation: The desire to recreate a moment of genius with dramatic lighting crosses into absurdist territory. The coworker's stage-direction ('turn the light on, like you just had an idea') and Ben's completely willing participation is wonderfully strange. It suggests these accountants are not just professionally reverent but have developed a full myth-making apparatus around Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, let's play a game. Who wants to keep score?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'll do it!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Actually, I think I should keep score.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No way, give it to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm keeping the score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Guys, guys, I clearly have the best handwriting. I should keep score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hold on, I'm very organized. This is my thing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, maybe we should just... not play this game.

jokes.text: Great idea... that we had a month ago. / The problem is, the trust still has claim to the property. / Then we dissolve the trust. / ...We never thought of that.
jokes.setup: Ben is working on a complex legal/financial case. He makes a suggestion.
jokes.punchline: His first idea gets immediately one-upped ('we had that a month ago'), then his second idea — dissolving the trust — stumps his experienced colleagues ('we never thought of that'), confirming his intellect while the first deflation was a red herring.
jokes.explanation: Good two-step structure — the fake-out of having his first idea dismissed sets up the genuine triumph of his second idea. 'We never thought of that' from people who've been on the case for months confirms Ben's competence in a satisfying way.

jokes.text: Maybe we name part of the park the 'Jamm Zone'? How about if in the Jamm zone, there's no married chicks allowed? Caution, Jeremy.
jokes.setup: Chris tries to broker a deal by suggesting naming part of the park after Jamm.
jokes.punchline: Jamm immediately specifies the Jamm Zone should exclude 'married chicks' — a blatantly sexist and legally problematic stipulation, which Chris gently handles with 'Caution, Jeremy.'
jokes.explanation: Jamm's park zone terms are predictably Jamm — the 'no married chicks' policy is funny in its absurd specificity. Chris's diplomatic 'Caution, Jeremy' — using his first name for extra gravity — is a nice touch. The joke lands on Jamm's consistent character.

jokes.text: Now I want you to be very careful about eating these. You eat the shells, and you throw the seeds out.
jokes.setup: Jamm serves edamame, calling them 'authentic edamame, or Tokyo beans.'
jokes.punchline: His instructions for eating edamame are completely backwards — you eat the seeds (beans), not the shells. His confident authority on 'Asian culture' is entirely wrong.
jokes.explanation: This is great cringe comedy with perfect character integration. Jamm presents wrong edamame instructions with total confidence — he doesn't know he's wrong, which makes it perfect. 'Authentic edamame, or Tokyo beans' positions him as an authority. Anyone who has eaten edamame gets the joke immediately.

jokes.text: Wow. You have really immersed yourself in Asian culture.
jokes.setup: Jamm finishes his edamame instructions.
jokes.punchline: Chris's 'Wow, you have really immersed yourself in Asian culture' is delivered with his characteristic sincere tone — it reads as genuine admiration but functions as irony, since Jamm's 'immersion' is demonstrably fake and wrong.
jokes.explanation: Chris's delivery makes this work — his diplomatic enthusiasm always teeters between genuine and ironic. Applied to Jamm's backwards edamame instructions, it reads as barely-veiled mockery. A good straight-man beat.

jokes.text: Ugh, Lezzie. Come on, I'm getting bored.
jokes.setup: Negotiations continue. Jamm is losing patience.
jokes.punchline: 'Lezzie' as Jamm's nickname for Leslie is a signature Jamm insult — lazy, contemptuous, a shorthand for everything obnoxious about him.
jokes.explanation: The nickname itself isn't clever, but it's a Jamm signature and consistently character-true. Functional, not inspired.

jokes.text: I did. And kudos on that pronunciation.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Jamm enjoys karaoke, carefully pronouncing it 'kah-rah-OH-kee.'
jokes.punchline: Jamm's 'kudos on that pronunciation' treats correct pronunciation as an achievement worthy of praise — suggesting he's encountered many people who get it wrong, or that he himself finds it impressive.
jokes.explanation: Nice small beat. The suggestion that karaoke pronunciation is an accomplishment worth crediting is a small window into Jamm's particular brand of cultural engagement (see also: backwards edamame). Economy is the strength here.

jokes.text: I remembered your favorite duet. Maybe it's time to take this party to Rydell High. Whoa! I cannot wait to hear your Travolta. Oh, no, no, no. I'm Sandra Dee. That's more of my register. You're Zuko.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests karaoke negotiations and reveals she knows Jamm's favorite duet.
jokes.punchline: Jamm eagerly anticipates being Travolta (Danny Zuko, the cool rebel); Leslie corrects him — she's Sandra Dee, and he's Zuko — which he accepts without question.
jokes.explanation: Leslie researching Jamm's karaoke preferences to use against him in negotiations is both funny and extremely Leslie. Her precision about 'that's more of my register' for Sandra Dee is delightful — she's thought about vocal range in this context. Jamm's easy acceptance of the Zuko role is a small character beat.

jokes.text: No, no, no. I'm Sandra Dee. That's more of my register. / You're Zuko.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Jamm are about to perform 'Summer Nights' from Grease.
jokes.punchline: Jamm insisting on playing Sandra Dee (the female role) because it's 'more of his register,' and Leslie assigning him Zuko — defying his preference — is a quick, character-perfect power reversal. Jamm's vocal register concern is also an unexpected, specific detail.
jokes.explanation: Jamm wanting to play Sandra Dee because of his vocal register — not because of any gender reason — is a funny, specific, unexpected characterization. Leslie's flat 'You're Zuko' refuses his request with complete authority. A small but perfectly calibrated joke.

jokes.text: I would like to buy five DVDs of this. No, 20. No, 60! No, that's insane. 20.
jokes.setup: Chris is watching Leslie and Jamm perform karaoke.
jokes.punchline: Chris's escalating desire for DVDs of the performance — 5 → 20 → 60 → back to 20 — mirrors his impulsive enthusiasm, punctuated by the self-correction ('No, that's insane') before settling on a still-excessive 20.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke with perfect Chris energy. The self-correction at 60 ('No, that's insane') only to land on 20 — still insane — is the punchline within the punchline. Chris's enthusiasm for human moments often tips into mania, and this captures that beautifully. Very quotable structure.

jokes.text: Glamping is 'glamour camping.' Heated tents, catered meals, wi-fi-- / You're describing a hotel.
jokes.setup: Tom explains that a developer wants to build a 'glamp-ground' on Ron's cabin land.
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat 'You're describing a hotel' punctures the entire concept of glamping in four words.
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson's four-word dismantling of the glamping concept is a pitch-perfect joke. It requires no setup beyond the definition Tom provides, and it's both logically accurate and a character statement. Economy is nearly perfect — 9.5. This is the kind of dry, instantly quotable line that becomes a shorthand for the character. Justifies high scores because it's effortless, true, and character-perfect.

jokes.text: The open house is now closed. We are not accepting bids at this time. The sun sets in 95 minutes. Good day.
jokes.setup: A hipster has just patronizingly commented on Ron's mustache.
jokes.punchline: Ron ends the open house on the spot — because of the mustache comment — with formal ceremonial language ('The open house is now closed. We are not accepting bids.') plus the extremely specific and irrelevant detail about sunset timing.
jokes.explanation: Ron ending the open house over a mustache comment is a perfect Ron moment — his dignity cannot be purchased at any price, including an over-asking bid. The formal language of 'we are not accepting bids' (using the royal 'we') and 'the sun sets in 95 minutes' as a formal goodbye justifies 8+. The 95-minute sunset detail is hilariously precise and suggests Ron has calculated exactly how many minutes of daylight remain. Deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, man. I love the mustache. So funny. You ever think about twisting it up at the ends, huh? Use a little beeswax? The open house is now closed. We are not accepting bids at this time. The sun sets in 95 minutes. Good day.
jokes.setup: A hipster buyer compliments Ron's mustache in an overly familiar, ironic way.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately closes the open house in response — the mustache comment was the final straw. 'The sun sets in 95 minutes. Good day.' is delivered with total Ron gravitas.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ron moments. The hipster treating Ron's mustache as a quirky ironic accessory and suggesting beeswax styling is exactly the kind of condescension Ron cannot tolerate. His response — immediately closing the entire open house, citing the sunset like a formal dismissal — is perfect escalation. 'The sun sets in 95 minutes. Good day.' would be the title of a Ron Swanson self-help book.

jokes.text: That's part of the charm of this whole place — the cantankerous old coot who owns it. It's authentic!
jokes.setup: Ron has just kicked everyone out.
jokes.punchline: The hipster misreads Ron's genuine irritation as performative 'authenticity' — ironically loving the thing Ron does in his genuine desire to get rid of them.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Ron's authentic rage is processed by the hipster as curated authenticity — you can't win. The irony of genuine behavior being consumed as performance is a sharp cultural observation layered on the character comedy.

jokes.text: I gotta say, that was pretty fun up there. We have fun when we collaborate, right? Working together? Lockbox, right?
jokes.setup: After karaoke, Jamm seems genuinely warmed up.
jokes.punchline: He builds toward the lockbox in the most transparent possible way — 'We have fun when we collaborate, right? Working together? Lockbox, right?' — a comedy of labored implication.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's attempt at a subtle pivot — followed immediately by literally just saying 'Lockbox, right?' — undercuts any pretense of subtlety. The joke is in how transparent his social manipulation is.

jokes.text: You know, in some weird, perverted, sexual way, I'm gonna miss you when you're gone. Oh. You are my Nemesis.
jokes.setup: Jamm expresses unexpected sentimentality about Leslie leaving.
jokes.punchline: He qualifies the sentiment as 'weird, perverted, sexual' — a word salad that undermines any genuine warmth — and then re-establishes their relationship as nemeses.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's inability to express warmth without immediately corrupting it with 'perverted, sexual' is peak character. The nemesis declaration is both earnest and absurd. It's an unexpected emotional beat handled in Jamm's inimitable way.

jokes.text: You're the Superman to my Lex Luthor. You want to be Lex Luthor? Uh, yeah. Lex Luthor is rich.
jokes.setup: Jamm assigns Leslie the Superman role and takes Lex Luthor for himself.
jokes.punchline: Leslie is surprised he'd choose the villain; Jamm's reasoning — 'Lex Luthor is rich' — is both an impeccable Jamm value statement and a defensible position.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jamm joke. 'Lex Luthor is rich' as a complete and sufficient reason to choose villainy is both funny and a precise character revelation — Jamm isn't embarrassed to be the bad guy as long as the bad guy has money. The structure is clean: setup (he picks villain), subversion (why?), punchline (wealth, obviously). Highly quotable.

jokes.text: And who sides with Lex Luthor, by the way? You probably watch Million Dollar Baby and root for the stool.
jokes.setup: Leslie is challenging Jamm's Lex Luthor preference.
jokes.punchline: 'You probably watch Million Dollar Baby and root for the stool' — an absurdist escalation that reimagines the worst possible sports fan (rooting for the inanimate object that injures the hero).
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and one of the best lines in Parks and Recreation. 'You probably watch Million Dollar Baby and root for the stool' is a perfect insult: (1) It's creative — no one would think of this. (2) It requires knowledge of the film (the character is paralyzed by a stool), making it a reward for the audience. (3) It's an escalation of the Superman/villain metaphor into something completely unexpected. (4) It has perfect economy — one sentence, devastating. (5) It's pure Leslie — passionate, pop-culture-literate, and slightly unhinged in her righteousness. This is an 'anchor example' level joke.

jokes.text: I haven't seen it. Not a big Morgan Freeman guy. I find his voice very grating.
jokes.setup: Leslie deploys a Million Dollar Baby reference as a devastating insult.
jokes.punchline: Jamm deflates the entire insult by not having seen it — and compounds it with the incomprehensible opinion that Morgan Freeman's voice is 'very grating.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect anti-punchline. Leslie's devastating insult lands on someone who has never seen the movie, which defuses it completely — AND Jamm adds the kicker that Morgan Freeman's voice is grating, an opinion so wrong it circles back to being funny. This is a rare double-punch: Leslie's joke (excellent) and Jamm's response (also excellent). The episode's funniest exchange.

jokes.text: I am leaving now. I am not moving. I'm just going home.
jokes.setup: After the emotional conversation about Ann's move, Leslie makes a declaration.
jokes.punchline: She clarifies she meant physically leaving the room — not 'moving' as in relocating — a small self-correction that shows how much Ann's departure is on her mind.
jokes.explanation: The preemptive clarification 'I am not moving, I'm just going home' suggests the word 'moving' has become loaded for Leslie. It's a sweet/funny beat at the edge of the emotional scene.

jokes.text: Are you guys coming back to my place? What's-- what's-- or are you guys going back to-- we wrapping up the weekend?
jokes.setup: Leslie and Chris turn to leave Jamm's house after the emotional scene.
jokes.punchline: Jamm, left alone, frantically tries to create reasons for them to stay — his loneliness revealed through rapid-fire incomplete invitations.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's frantic 'we wrapping up the weekend?' as Leslie and Chris leave is a surprisingly effective character beat — his wife is gone, his nemesis is leaving Pawnee, and he doesn't want to be alone. Played for laughs but with genuine pathos underneath.

jokes.text: Ann arbor sounds disgusting. / She already has family there.
jokes.setup: Chris tells Leslie that Ann has signed a lease in Ann Arbor.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's protest 'Ann arbor sounds disgusting' — rejecting a city based solely on its name — is followed by Chris's patient practical response, treating her objection as legitimate.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's denial-based objections to Michigan are funny as a series. 'Sounds disgusting' as a city assessment is childlike in a way that's characteristically Leslie when she's upset.

jokes.text: Surprise pizza party! Wait a second. That's not pizza. Those are calzones! I love calzones! We know!
jokes.setup: Ben's coworkers throw him a party for cracking the case.
jokes.punchline: The 'pizza party' is actually calzones — Ben's preference is known and catered to. His delight and their knowing 'We know!' reveals this is carefully researched Ben-appreciation.
jokes.explanation: The calzone detail is endearing and funny — it's specific, character-consistent (Ben's calzone love is an established quirk), and the 'We know!' suggests the coworkers have done their research on their idol. A warm character moment with genuine comedic heat.

jokes.text: I think it's safe to say I made the right choice.
jokes.setup: Ben surveys the calzone celebration around him.
jokes.punchline: His talking-head conclusion that he made 'the right choice' — knowing we'll immediately learn he's about to quit — sets up the dramatic irony of the next scene.
jokes.explanation: Works primarily as dramatic irony on rewatch — Ben saying this right before quitting is the joke. On first viewing, it's mildly funny; on second viewing, it's a well-placed plant.

jokes.text: That was that couple you liked at the open house. I despised them. Well, they just came back with a new offer and jacked that shizz up. Way over asking price.
jokes.setup: Tom gets a call during the negotiation about Ron's cabin.
jokes.punchline: Tom's description of Ron's reception of the hipster buyers as 'liked' when Ron clearly despised them is a nice ironic beat; the news that their offer is way over asking is the comedic payoff — Ron's contempt accidentally drove up the price.
jokes.explanation: The irony that Ron's authentic cantankerousness — his attempt to drive buyers away — made the hipsters love the cabin more and bid over asking is a satisfying structural joke. Tom's reframe of 'despised' as 'liked' is a nice throw.

jokes.text: I can't even understand what you're saying right now. That cabin served an important purpose for me, as a quiet refuge from the nonsense of modern life. I'd like the next owners to understand and share that purpose.
jokes.setup: Tom can't comprehend Ron not taking an over-asking offer on a cabin he bought for $2,200.
jokes.punchline: Ron's eloquent, sincere statement of purpose — refusing to sell to people who don't understand the cabin's meaning — is comedic because it's so extravagantly principled about a property transaction.
jokes.explanation: Tom's financial bewilderment versus Ron's philosophical stance is a classic character-contrast joke. Ron's language ('quiet refuge from the nonsense of modern life') is almost poetic, making it funnier against Tom's 'I can't even understand what you're saying right now.'

jokes.text: Ron, who cares who they are? That's a massive bid. / I bought that cabin 18 years ago for $2,200.
jokes.setup: Donna is trying to convince Ron to take the huge offer from the developers.
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals the original purchase price — $2,200 — which contextualizes his complete indifference to money. To someone who paid $2,200, any massive bid feels like surplus.
jokes.explanation: The $2,200 detail is a perfect Ron Swanson number — cheap enough to be funny, specific enough to be real. It suggests he bought it in the '90s at a price that reflects his indifference to property as investment. Good character economy.

jokes.text: I'll buy it. You can't afford that house. Can you afford that house?
jokes.setup: Ron explains he wants a buyer who shares his cabin's purpose.
jokes.punchline: April immediately volunteers to buy. Tom and Donna share her financial reality check as a near-simultaneous reaction.
jokes.explanation: April's impulsive 'I'll buy it' followed by the double-skepticism of Tom and Donna is a good quick beat. April's desire to escape to a remote cabin to look at spiders and contemplate murder makes perfect sense for her character.

jokes.text: I'd go up there and take Andy and Champion and just get away from everyone else and look at spiders. And it's where I'd bury the bodies of that annoying couple after I murder them.
jokes.setup: April is asked what she'd use the cabin for.
jokes.punchline: Her plan escalates from wholesome (Andy and Champion, looking at spiders) to premeditated murder of the annoying hipster couple — delivered without tonal shift.
jokes.explanation: Classic April Ludgate escalation: a genuinely sweet vision (cabin with Andy and the dog) pivots instantly to detailed murder plans. The casual specificity of 'bury the bodies of that annoying couple' — naming her target and burial site in one sentence — is perfect April. The tonal continuity (no shift between spiders and murder) is the key technique.

jokes.text: Here's my offer. I will give you everything in my purse. $8, a bunch of loose cough drops, and Larry's asthma inhaler.
jokes.setup: April wants to make a formal offer on Ron's cabin.
jokes.punchline: Her 'offer' is the literal contents of her purse: $8, loose cough drops, and a coworker's stolen medical device.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The list is perfectly constructed: $8 (pitifully small), loose cough drops (bizarre as currency), and Larry's asthma inhaler (a stolen medical device with a specific victim). The escalation from small to random to stolen medical equipment is impeccable. April treating this as a serious real estate offer is pure character. High quotability and rewatch value.

jokes.text: Thank God. I've been looking for that. Larry, this is part of a real estate transaction now. You have no legal claim to it. Sorry, I had no idea.
jokes.setup: April's offer includes Larry's asthma inhaler.
jokes.punchline: Larry is relieved to see his inhaler but is immediately shut down by Donna's legal ruling that it's now part of a real estate transaction. Larry's meek 'Sorry, I had no idea' is the capper.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of April's absurd offer into a legally binding transaction — with Donna solemnly declaring Larry has 'no legal claim' to his own asthma inhaler — is a perfect Parks and Rec joke. The show's comedy often comes from treating absurd situations with bureaucratic seriousness. Larry's apologetic 'Sorry, I had no idea' about his own medical device is quintessential Larry comedy.

jokes.text: This is the best offer I've heard yet. Uh, you tripping right now. Sold. Don't even trip.
jokes.setup: Ron considers April's $8-plus-cough-drops offer.
jokes.punchline: Ron accepts — rejecting an over-asking-price offer for cash, in favor of $8 and medical waste — because April is the right buyer.
jokes.explanation: Ron's 'Sold' — delivered with the same gravity as any of his major pronouncements — applied to an $8 real estate transaction is excellent. Tom's 'you tripping right now' and Donna's 'don't even trip' create a perfect call-and-response around Ron's insane decision. Only Ron would find April Ludgate the ideal cabin heir.

jokes.text: Your commission. Your share, mogul.
jokes.setup: The sale is concluded for $8.
