jokes.punchline: Donna and Tom solemnly exchange commission shares from an $8 sale — treating the split of cents as a significant financial transaction.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Tom's mogul aspirations — 'your share, mogul' — applied to a 5% commission on $8 (approximately 40 cents) is a quietly excellent joke. The seriousness with which both parties treat this exchange is the punchline. 'Mogul' now has devastating irony.

jokes.text: I'm about to play golf with a guy who was almost on The Apprentice, so this better be good.
jokes.setup: Chris approaches Jamm with an offer.
jokes.punchline: 'Almost on The Apprentice' as a status marker — Jamm's social circle is defined by near-celebrity proximity to minor reality TV.
jokes.explanation: 'Almost on The Apprentice' is a perfectly calibrated status detail for Jamm — close enough to celebrity to be impressed by, sad enough to be funny. The casualness with which he name-drops this non-achievement as a scheduling conflict is excellent character economy.

jokes.text: Well, vote passed. 3-2.
jokes.setup: The lockbox vote happens off-screen; we cut to the result.
jokes.punchline: The completely flat delivery of '3-2' — after all the episode's machinations — undercuts the drama with total bureaucratic blandness.
jokes.explanation: The structural joke of ending a major episode arc with the flattest possible official proclamation is mildly funny — the comedy of anticlimax. Limited on its own but works in context.

jokes.text: Jamm is gonna be so pissed when he finds out that you're leaving and your I.O.U.s are worthless.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Chris celebrate the lockbox victory.
jokes.punchline: Chris cheerfully anticipates Jamm's fury — a small dark delight from the normally diplomatic city manager.
jokes.explanation: Chris's barely-contained glee at Jamm's impending rage is a nice character beat — he's allowed himself this small deviation from diplomacy. Works as a moment more than a joke.

jokes.text: Well, it's not the most ethical thing that I've ever done, but on the flip side, Jamm is a big, mean dope.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Chris is comfortable with the ethically questionable I.O.U. scheme.
jokes.punchline: Chris's ethical framework: 'not most ethical' is balanced by 'Jamm is a big, mean dope' — as if being a dope is a sufficient moral counterweight.
jokes.explanation: 'Big, mean dope' as an ethical justification is funny for its childlike vocabulary — Chris usually speaks in the language of wellness and positivity, and this registers as a rare lapse into playground insult. Good character beat.

jokes.text: Speaking of which, how's the new gig coming? Well, I got a raise, and my fridge is full of calzones, so not complaining.
jokes.setup: Discussion of the new job.
jokes.punchline: Ben's measure of job satisfaction: a raise is mentioned in the same breath as a fridge full of calzones — the two are presented as equivalent professional metrics.
jokes.explanation: The calzone callback works well here — Ben's job satisfaction is measured in calzones. Warm and character-consistent. 'So not complaining' as an understatement when you have a raise AND unlimited calzones is a nice note.

jokes.text: And I've talked to some people, and you have the votes if you want the job. Wh-- Seriously? Is this for realskis? This is 100% certified for realskis.
jokes.setup: Chris offers Ben the city manager job.
jokes.punchline: 'For realskis' — Ben's slang term for 'for real' — is a delightful Wyatt-ism, and Chris's adoption of it ('100% certified for realskis') plays as genuine warmth.
jokes.explanation: 'For realskis' is a good Ben Wyatt coinage — the suffix '-skis' applied to 'real' has a specific nerdy-enthusiastic energy. Chris's 'certified' amplification is a sweet beat.

jokes.text: Wyatt, you're late. I'm just kidding, you can do whatever you want.
jokes.setup: Ben arrives at the accounting firm on what turns out to be his last day.
jokes.punchline: Barney sets up a normal boss dynamic ('you're late'), then immediately undermines it with 'you can do whatever you want' — because Ben is so beloved he is exempt from normal rules.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Ben-is-a-god-here dynamic. 'You can do whatever you want' as a boss statement is a nice reversal. Works well as part of the running accounting firm joke.

jokes.text: Actually, Barney, I'm afraid I have some bad news. Today's my last day. I got an opportunity I couldn't say no to, and I have to quit. Again. No need to explain. I knew it was too good to be true.
jokes.setup: Ben is about to quit the accounting firm on his first day of his second stint.
jokes.punchline: Barney's 'I knew it was too good to be true' — resigned acceptance of Ben's recurring pattern of quitting — is both sad and funny. His 'no need to explain' suggests this is a familiar conversation.
jokes.explanation: 'I knew it was too good to be true' is the perfect resignation for someone who has been burned by Ben's commitment before. The gentle acceptance rather than anger makes it funnier. 'Again' as Ben's self-aware appendage ('quit. Again.') is a good beat.

jokes.text: 'You can play with one warrior, but it's just not nearly as good. Enjoy. Ben Wyatt.' Let's play. I call ledgerman! No.
jokes.setup: Ben leaves a going-away gift in the break room — the Cones of Dunshire game.
jokes.punchline: The coworkers immediately embrace the game. The callback to ledgerman from the cold open — with someone eagerly claiming it and being denied — circles back to the episode's opening joke perfectly.
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant episode closer. The Cones of Dunshire was introduced as an absurd product of Ben's free time that would be 'thrown in the garbage' — and it ends up in the hands of the people who most appreciate it. 'I call ledgerman! No.' is a perfect button: the most coveted/mocked role from the opening lands as the final punchline. The note 'you can play with one warrior but it's just not nearly as good' is a lovely Ben-specific coda.

tmdb_overview: Leslie comes to terms with her last day in office and plans for the future with Ben. Chris and Ann find out the sex of their child, Andy comes home from London, and Tom looks to the future.
insight: Board game design obsession drives 56 jokes across a surprisingly dense, character-driven half hour.
